cards.title: Optimal-size highly unbalanced lossless expanders
cards.formal:
Do there exist two fixed deterministic algorithms \(P,Q\) and positive integers \(C,c\) with the following properties for every pair of integers \(N,K\) satisfying \(N\ge2\) and \(1\le K\le N\)? Write \(L_{N}=1+\lceil\log_{2} N\rceil\). Algorithm \(P\), on input \((N,K)\), must output positive integers \(D=D(N,K)\) and \(M=M(N,K)\) such that
\[
D\le C L_{N}^{c},\qquad M\le CKD.
\]
Algorithm \(Q\), on input \((N,K,x,j)\) with \(x\in[N]\) and \(j\in[D]\), must output an element \(\Gamma_{N,K}(x,j)\in[M]\). Both the parameter computation and each neighbor computation must take at most \(C L_{N}^{c}\) steps in the uniform bit model defined below. The resulting bipartite multigraph must satisfy
\[
\forall S\subseteq[N],\quad |S|=K\ \Longrightarrow
\left|\{\Gamma_{N,K}(x,j):x\in S,\ j\in[D]\}\right|
\ge\frac{99}{100}DK.
\]
Thus the target is a fully explicit family with polylogarithmic left degree, a right side of size at most a constant times \(KD\), and expansion for every left set of size exactly \(K\). The algorithms and constants are chosen before \(N,K\); they must work uniformly over the entire stated parameter range. Prove this existence statement or its negation.
cards.why: Lossless expansion preserves almost all distinct choices made from an arbitrary input set while compressing their range. A construction with this right-side size and fast neighbor computation would provide lossless condensers with constant entropy overhead, improving a basic resource used in randomness extraction, coding and related algorithms.
cards.status_note: Vadhan’s December 2012 monograph explicitly poses the recovered exact-K construction target. Individual primary-source reading and bounded subsequent checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching construction or refutation: the checked constant-gap condenser has a larger seed bound, the 2026 two-sided construction retains a larger right side, and the 13 September 2026 preprint gives a different expansion factor. Retain as source-open, with the uniform bit-model conventions disclosed; this is not an exhaustive verification of present openness or a claim to have checked every cited proof.

progress.text: Theorem 5.35 gives fully explicit lossless expansion with \(D=\operatorname{poly}(\log N)\) and \(M\le D^{2}K^{1+\alpha}\) for each fixed \(\alpha>0\) and fixed error; Open Problem 5.36 asks to reduce the right side to \(O(KD)\). The same discussion notes that the desired right-side size is known with a quasipolynomial rather than polynomial dependence of the degree on \(\log N\).

Kalev and Ta-Shma’s Theorem 2 has condenser output length \(m\le d+(1+\alpha)k_{\max}\), improving the earlier \(2d+(1+\alpha)k_{\max}\) term subject to their parameter restrictions. With \(K=2^{k_{\max}}\) and \(D=2^d\), this corresponds to \(M\le DK^{1+\alpha}\); a fixed positive \(\alpha\) still leaves a growing factor beyond \(KD\).

Cook and Moshkovitz’s Theorem 5 constructs invertible lossless condensers with \(m=k+d+O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) and \(d=O((\log(n/\varepsilon))^3)\) in its stated error range. For fixed error and \(N=2^n\), the right side has order \(KD\), but the degree is bounded by \(2^{O((\log\log N)^3)}\), which does not provide the requested polynomial bound in \(\log N\).

Chattopadhyay, Gurumukhani, Ringach and Zhao publish a two-sided lossless-expansion result. Their Theorem 2 has \(K=N^{\delta}\), polylogarithmic left degree and \(M\ge N^{1.01\delta-o(1)}\) for fixed positive \(\delta\), so its right side exceeds \(O(KD)\). The additional expansion from the right side does not settle the stated size target.

Bauwens and Zimand’s preprint constructs explicit unbalanced graphs with nearly optimal right-side size and small degree for one-expansion: every set up to the designated size has at least as many neighbors as elements. Its Theorem 1.1 does not give the required \((99/100)D\) expansion factor.

sentences: The problem asks for an explicit bipartite graph for every left-side size and every prescribed exact subset size.
Each such subset must reach at least ninety-nine percent of the maximum number of distinct neighbors allowed by the left degree.
The left degree must be polynomial in the logarithm of the left-side size, and the right side must have size at most a fixed constant times the subset size times that degree.
A single deterministic construction must compute its parameters and any requested neighbor in polylogarithmic time, making the graphs useful as lossless condensers.
A complete Lean proof must establish this uniform construction or its negation, while the checked later results do not meet all of its requirements.

cards.definitions:
For a positive integer \(t\), \([t]=\{1,\ldots,t\}\). The two vertex classes are disjoint labeled copies of \([N]\) and \([M]\). Each left vertex \(x\) has precisely \(D\) edge slots, indexed by \(j\in[D]\), whose right endpoints are \(\Gamma_{N,K}(x,j)\). Repeated right endpoints in different slots are allowed, so degree counts edges with multiplicity. In contrast, a neighborhood is a set of distinct right vertices, and its cardinality counts each right vertex once. No degree condition is imposed on right vertices.

For fixed \(N,K\), the graph must have the displayed expansion property simultaneously for all sets \(S\) with exactly \(K\) elements. It is not required to satisfy the same expansion factor for every smaller cardinality in that same graph. Different values of \(K\), including those with the same \(N\), may produce different graphs, degrees and right-side sizes. The factor \(99/100\) is fixed, not an input parameter. The target does not ask for an optimal exponent in the degree bound. There is no extra condition \(M<N\); the full source parameter range includes values of \(K\) for which such an imbalance cannot hold.

Use ordinary binary representations of nonnegative integers, with no leading zeros and with zero represented by the single digit 0. Encode a tuple by these representations separated by the symbol \(\#\), with no trailing separator. Input and output alphabets contain the fixed symbols 0, 1 and \(\#\); the number of symbols is a bit-length measure up to a fixed constant factor. Algorithm \(P\) outputs the tuple \((D,M)\), and \(Q\) outputs one binary integer. Inputs are supplied between end markers on a read-only input tape. Each algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes and an output tape. Each transition reads and writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell; one transition is one time step. All parameter selection, arithmetic, work-tape access and output writing count toward the time bound. There are no random bits, advice strings, oracles or uncharged preprocessing.

The running-time requirements are worst-case bounds on every valid input just specified, including every valid vertex and edge-slot query. No behavior is required on malformed tuples or tuples outside the promises. Each neighbor query starts with blank work tapes and may recompute parameters within its time allowance; no graph-sized data structure is supplied. Thus the representation is an implicit neighbor function, not a demand to output all \(ND\) edge slots in polylogarithmic time.

The positive constants \(C,c\) do not depend on \(N,K,x,j\), or on the set \(S\). Using one constant and one exponent for the degree and both computation bounds, and the same constant in \(M\le CKD\), is a normalization: separate fixed polynomial and multiplicative bounds can all be enlarged to bounds of this form. The finite case \(N=1\) can be handled separately and has no effect on the construction question. The word lossless refers here to preserving at least the fraction \(99/100\) of the maximum possible \(DK\) distinct neighbors, rather than requiring that all edge endpoints be distinct.
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed uniform existence statement or its logical negation, using the specified machine model, graph representation and quantifier order.

For a positive answer, supply finite descriptions of \(P,Q\), constants \(C,c\ge1\), and proofs of the parameter-output requirements, both time bounds, valid neighbor outputs and the expansion inequality for every admissible \(N,K\) and every exact-size set \(S\). All constants must be uniform in the input parameters.

For a negative answer, define \(\operatorname{Good}(P,Q,C,c;N,K)\) to mean all the displayed parameter, computation and expansion requirements for that pair \((N,K)\), and prove
\[
\forall P,Q\ \forall C,c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists N,K\in\mathbb Z,
\quad N\ge2\ \land\ 1\le K\le N\ \land\
\neg\operatorname{Good}(P,Q,C,c;N,K).
\]
The quantifiers over \(P,Q\) range over all deterministic machines of the defined kind. The failure can be in the uniform construction or resource requirements; it need not show that a graph with those numerical parameters fails to exist. A nonconstructive family, a slower construction, a construction for only selected parameter pairs, or a guarantee of only one distinct neighbor per left vertex does not meet the full positive criterion. The fixed fraction \(99/100\) is part of the proposition, not a numerical-answer tolerance.

context_blocks.text: Vadhan’s Open Problem 5.36 asks for expansion of sets of size exactly \(K\), with fixed expansion factor \(0.99D\), polylogarithmic degree and \(M=O(KD)\).

This card makes the source’s fully explicit interpretation concrete through uniform deterministic bit algorithms for the parameters and individual neighbors, while allowing parallel edges and keeping all constants independent of \(N,K\).
The monograph restates the target as a lossless condenser with logarithmic seed length and constant entropy overhead, explaining its role in processing weak randomness.
Kalev and Ta-Shma improve the polynomially larger right-side bound of earlier constructions, whereas Cook and Moshkovitz obtain constant entropy overhead with a larger seed-length guarantee.
The checked September 2026 two-sided and one-expansion results concern different parameter guarantees, and the bounded review found no construction or refutation meeting the full target.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.
